text: Mathematical notation looks like a secret code, but it is really shorthand, written by people who got tired of saying the same long sentence over and over. Every formula in this course is a set of instructions that you could type as a few lines of Python, so in this lesson we learn to read the pieces of shorthand that appear most often.

Start with a list of numbers called x. Rather than giving each entry its own name, we write x with a small number hanging below it, called a subscript, which works exactly like a house number on a street. x sub one is the first house, x sub two is the second, and x sub i means whichever house you happen to be standing at. In Python that is simply x in square brackets, with one caveat, which is that Python counts its houses from zero.

When a whole list is treated as a single object, it is usually printed as a bold letter, or as a letter with a small arrow on top, and its entries are the same letter in plain type with subscripts. So bold x is the vector, the whole street, while x sub i is a single house on it. Keeping those two apart is half the battle when you read a formula.

Now the sigma sign, a capital Greek S that stands for sum. Read it as a loop written vertically. Underneath it you find where the counter starts, above it you find where the counter stops, and to its right is the thing you add on each pass. So the sum from i equals one to n of x sub i says: let i walk from the first house to the last, pick up the value at each house, and keep a running total.

In Python, that sentence becomes a running total that starts at zero, a for loop over the positions, and one line that adds the current entry to the total. The loop counter plays the part of the subscript, and the body of the loop is whatever stands to the right of the sigma.

The most important case for this course has two lists under one sigma, as in the sum of x sub i times y sub i. Notice that there is only one counter, i, and it appears in both places, so both lists are read at the same house at the same time: first entry with first entry, second with second. It is a single walk down two parallel streets, which in Python is one loop over zip of x and y, not a loop inside a loop. A nested loop would pair every house with every other house, and that is a different formula, with two counters, usually called i and j.

You have already met this exact formula under another name. The sum of x sub i times y sub i is the dot product of the vectors x and y. Inside a language model, that one line runs an enormous number of times, whenever the model checks how well two words match, so reading it fluently will pay off again and again.

So a subscript picks out one entry, a bold letter names the whole list, and a sigma is a loop whose counter is the subscript. With that alphabet in hand, the mathematics can begin properly, and it begins where every language model begins, with vectors, which are arrows and lists of numbers at the same time.
